note_text: Research showing that labor share remains within historical ranges once accounting for depreciation and taxes is kept constant was published by Benjamin Bridgman of the BEA. Atkinson’s 2009 paper discusses the decline in labor share and policy responses. https://bea.gov/sites/default/files/papers/WP2014-10.pdf http://piketty.pse.ens.fr/files/Atkinson09.pdf
claim: Atkinson published a paper showing that if accounting methods are kept constant over time, labor share has not fallen.
context: Some might say labor share has been falling in the last 20 to 30 years. But there have been a lot of accounting changes in the last 30 to 40 years. For example, Atkinson has a paper showing that if you keep the accounting constant over the years, labor share hasn't even fallen ever.

source_verification.reasoning: Both sources directly support the note's claims: Bridgman's BEA paper supports the accounting-adjustment finding, and Atkinson's 2009 paper discusses labor share decline. The note correctly attributes the accounting research to Bridgman, correcting the post's misattribution to Atkinson.

citations.quote: I show that U.S. labor share has not fallen as much once items that do not add to capital, depreciation and production taxes, are netted out. Recent net labor share is within its historical range whereas gross share is at its lowest level.
citations.explanation: Supports the note's claim that Bridgman of the BEA showed labor share remains within historical ranges once depreciation and taxes are accounted for.
